When it ended, Farida said, "That one was short, can I watch the next one?" Yes again. Then, "Can I finish the season? Only a few are left." Ammi was cooking and said, "Hmm, okay." By the time the sun went down, Farida had watched the whole evening. Her homework was still in her bag. I don't think she planned it like a trick. Each step just seemed small after the one before. Ammi looked at the clock in surprise, as if she didn't know where the time had gone.

qa.q: Where was Farida's homework at the end of the evening?
qa.a: Still in her bag.

qa.q: Why might Ammi have looked at the clock in surprise?
qa.a: She had agreed to one small request at a time, so she hadn't noticed that the yeses added up to the whole evening.

qa.q: What could Ammi try next Sunday when Farida asks for "just one"?
qa.a: She could set the limit at the start, one cartoon and then homework, and at each new request ask whether she would agree if it were the first thing asked.

qa.q: How does Deepika see Farida's asking?
qa.a: Deepika doesn't think Farida planned a trick; to Deepika, each request simply seemed small after the one before it.

grounding: A sister watches a young girl ask her mother for one cartoon, then another, then the whole evening, each yes making the next feel natural.

subtype: Small request opens the way to a bigger one [Actor]
passage:
Monday: Jagdish finished his homework and asked, "Mummy, can I play my game for just ten minutes?" Preeti said yes. He stopped right on time.
Wednesday: "I stopped on time on Monday, right? So can I have twenty minutes today?" Preeti smiled. Twenty seemed fair.
Friday: "Mummy, I've had twenty every day. It's Friday. Can I play all evening, till dinner and after?" Preeti opened her mouth to say yes, then stopped. From ten minutes to the whole evening in five days, and each ask had felt so small. "If you'd asked for the whole evening on Monday, what would I have said?" Jagdish grinned. "No." "Then twenty minutes, and then cricket outside."

qa.q: How long did Jagdish first ask to play on Monday?
qa.a: Just ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish mention stopping on time when he asked for twenty minutes?
qa.a: He seemed to feel that Monday's yes, and his good behaviour, made a bigger request feel like the natural next step.

qa.q: What question did Preeti ask on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: "If you'd asked for the whole evening on Monday, what would I have said?" It made her judge Friday's request on its own, not as a small step after the others.

qa.q: What might Preeti have felt when she stopped herself on Friday?
qa.a: She seems a little startled at how ten minutes had grown to a whole evening in five days, since each ask had felt so small, so she settles on twenty minutes and cricket.

grounding: Over one week, a boy moves from asking for ten minutes of a game to the whole evening, each yes making the next request feel natural.

subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage:
Monday: Ojas clicked "I pledge to reduce plastic" on a campaign page. Just a name and an email. It felt good.
Wednesday: An email arrived: "Thank you, Ojas! Pledge-takers like you share with five friends." He forwarded it to five people, including Trisha.
Saturday: Another email: "Committed members like you volunteer for our weekend drive, collecting donations door to door. Can we count on you?" Ojas's stomach tightened. He had exams next week. But he was a pledge-taker now, a "committed member." Saying no felt like being a fake. He typed "Yes" and hovered over send. Trisha, reading over his shoulder, said, "You clicked one box on Monday. Would you have said yes if this was the first thing they asked?" Ojas deleted the "Yes."

qa.q: What did Ojas click on Monday?
qa.a: "I pledge to reduce plastic."

qa.q: Why did saying no on Saturday feel like "being a fake" to Ojas?
qa.a: He felt guilty and trapped: the emails called him a "committed member", so refusing seemed inconsistent with who he had claimed to be, even with exams next week.

qa.q: What question turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Trisha asked whether he would have said yes if this had been the first request; it separated the big ask from the small box he clicked on Monday.

qa.q: How might Trisha see the campaign's emails?
qa.a: Trisha, who received the forward, seems to notice how each email builds on the last to make the next ask feel natural, and cares enough to point it out.

grounding: A teenager who agreed to a small online pledge finds the larger follow-up hard to refuse, because saying no feels inconsistent with his earlier yes.

subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage: Kiran, before you sign up for more of those online challenges, hear your Baljeet Mama's story. At sixteen, I had just made my first email ID at the cyber café. A site asked me to sign an online pledge to "stand with farmers." One click. Easy. A week later they wrote, "As a pledger, will you donate fifty rupees?" Fifty rupees was my whole week's money, but how could a pledger say no? I paid. Then they asked me to get ten classmates to pay too, and to send my father's phone number for "updates." That's when my stomach turned. I told my father that same evening, and he asked, "Would you have given fifty rupees and my number to strangers on the first day?" No. Each yes had made the next one feel owed.

qa.q: How much did the site ask Baljeet to donate?
qa.a: Fifty rupees.

qa.q: Why did young Baljeet feel he couldn't refuse the donation?
qa.a: Baljeet felt torn and pressured: fifty rupees was his whole week's money, but having signed the pledge, saying no felt wrong for a "pledger".

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did young Baljeet do right?
qa.a: When they asked for his father's phone number, he felt uneasy and told his father that evening, whose question showed he would never have agreed on the first day.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's father have felt hearing about the requests?
qa.a: He may have been concerned that strangers wanted his number and his son's classmates' money, but he helped calmly with a simple question.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, as a teenager, a one-click online pledge made a bigger follow-up request feel impossible to refuse.

subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage: The wedding sangeet was deafening, Nilesh's phone was at six percent, and a notification said "Offer ends in 5 minutes." Last week he had tapped "I pledge: one screen-free hour a day" on a wellness page. Tiny, easy. Now they wrote: "Pledgers like you are serious about change. Get our 30-day Focus Journal, ₹499, only for committed members." Nilesh had exactly ₹600 of wedding gift money. Not buying felt like breaking his pledge. His thumb hovered. His cousin Tarun leaned over, shouting over the dhol, "What's that?" "I pledged. So I sort of have to." Tarun shouted back, "You pledged an hour off screens. Not ₹499!" The phone died in Nilesh's hand. He laughed, a bit relieved, and went to dance.

qa.q: How much was the Focus Journal?
Why did not buying the journal feel like breaking a pledge to Nilesh?
qa.a: The page called him a "committed member", so after the small pledge, refusing the bigger request felt inconsistent with who he had said he was.

qa.q: What point did Tarun make, and how could Nilesh use it next time?
qa.a: That the pledge was an hour off screens, not ₹499; next time Nilesh can ask whether he would agree to the new request if it were the first one.

qa.q: How might Tarun see the offer from outside?
qa.a: To Tarun, it is obvious the ₹499 journal has nothing to do with a screen-free hour; without the pledge feeling, the ask looks like plain selling.

grounding: A teenager who made a small online pledge feels bound to buy a pricier follow-up offer, because refusing seems inconsistent with his earlier yes.

subtype: Refusing a huge favour, then feeling bound by a smaller one [Receiver]
passage: Tanvir, you said yes to the society's "small favour" right after refusing the big one? Sit, and let your Sudha Phuphi tell you something. When I was twenty, our hostel senior asked me to run the entire annual fest. Every committee, every sponsor. I said no, firmly, and I was proud of myself. Then she sighed, looked hurt and said, "Fine, you're right, it's too much. Could you at least handle the food stalls?" I heard myself say yes before she had finished. She had given something up, so I felt I had to give something back. The food stalls meant three weeks of phone calls and one burnt tent. I never wanted the food stalls either. If she had asked me that first, I would have said no in one breath.

qa.q: What did the senior first ask Sudha to run?
qa.a: The entire annual fest.

qa.q: Why did young Sudha say yes to the food stalls before the senior finished?
qa.a: She felt guilty after refusing, because the senior had given something up and looked hurt, so a yes seemed owed in return.

qa.q: What question could young Sudha have asked before agreeing to the food stalls?
qa.a: Whether she would have agreed to the food stalls if that had been the first request; her own answer, no in one breath, would have freed her.

qa.q: Why might Phuphi be telling Tanvir this story now?
qa.a: Tanvir has just agreed to a "small favour" after refusing a big one, and Phuphi wants Tanvir to recognise the same pull she felt at twenty.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, at twenty, turning down a huge request made her feel bound to accept the smaller one that followed.

subtype: Refusing a huge favour, then feeling bound by a smaller one [Receiver]
passage: It was 9:55 p.m., the hostel gate closed at ten, and Abhinav was blocking the corridor. "Yusuf, lend me your scooter for the Goa trip. Just ten days." "No way. I need it for my internship." Abhinav's shoulders dropped. "Okay, okay, too much, you're right." Then, quickly: "Then just let me use it every evening this week. Only that." The warden's whistle blew. Yusuf felt a strange tug. Abhinav had backed down; it felt rude not to meet him halfway. "Fine, I guess," he started. Then he stopped. Would he have said yes if every evening this week had been the first ask? He needed those evenings for his project. "Actually, no. One evening. Thursday." He ran for the gate.

qa.q: When did the hostel gate close?
qa.a: At ten.

qa.q: What was the "strange tug" Yusuf felt?
qa.a: After Abhinav backed down from the big request, Yusuf felt he ought to meet him halfway and agree to the smaller one, as if he owed it.

qa.q: What choice did Yusuf make before running for the gate, and why was it sound?
qa.a: He asked whether he would agree to every evening as a first request, saw he needed those evenings for his project, and offered only Thursday.

qa.q: How might the asking look from Abhinav's side?
qa.a: Abhinav may truly need the scooter and not be planning any trick; backing down and asking for less may simply feel reasonable to him.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young man who refused a big request feels bound to accept the smaller compromise that follows, before checking it on its own.

subtype: Refusing a huge favour, then feeling bound by a smaller one [Receiver]
passage: In Rashmi's one-room flat in Lajpat Nagar, her phone buzzed. Her cousin Yash. "Rashmi, can six of my friends stay at your place during my wedding week? Please?" She looked at her single mattress and her exam timetable. "Yash, no. I'm sorry. My exams are that week." A long pause. Then: "Totally understand. Too much. Okay, then can I at least keep their luggage at yours for the month? Only eight bags." Eight bags would cover the whole floor. Rashmi's thumb moved toward "ok" anyway. He had accepted her no so nicely. Wasn't it her turn to give something? She sat on the mattress, the phone warm in her hand, feeling guilty and cornered at once.

qa.q: How many bags did Yash want to keep at Rashmi's flat?
qa.a: Eight bags.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling as her thumb moved toward "ok"?
qa.a: She felt guilty and cornered at once; because Yash accepted her no so nicely, she felt she owed him a yes, even though the bags would cover her floor.

qa.q: What could Rashmi ask herself before replying?
qa.a: Whether she would agree to eight bags for a month if that had been Yash's first request; if not, she can kindly say no to this too.

qa.q: How might Yash see the luggage request?
qa.a: Yash may think it's a small, fair compromise after the big no, without noticing it would fill Rashmi's floor during her exams.

grounding: After refusing a cousin's big request, a young woman feels an urge to accept the smaller compromise, as if it is now her turn to give.

subtype: Asking whether it would be a yes as a first request [Response]
passage:
Hi Darshan,
Thanks for understanding when I said no to leading the whole client migration. When you then asked if I could "just" own the weekend testing for it, I almost said yes on the spot. It felt like you had met me halfway. But I slept on it and asked myself one question: if weekend testing had been your first request, would I have agreed? Honestly, no. I've promised my weekends this month to my mother's physiotherapy visits. So I'm saying no to this step too, and I hope that's okay. I can review the test plan on Monday mornings, if that helps.
Warmly,
Urmila

qa.q: What did Darshan ask Urmila to "just" own?
qa.a: The weekend testing for the client migration.

qa.q: Why did Urmila almost say yes on the spot?
qa.a: Urmila felt a pull of guilt: after refusing the big request, it seemed Darshan had met Urmila halfway, so a yes felt owed in return.

qa.q: What question helped Urmila decide, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: "If weekend testing had been your first request, would I have agreed?" The honest no, because of the physiotherapy visits, led Urmila to decline and offer something that fits: Monday reviews.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel reading the email?
qa.a: Darshan might be disappointed about the weekends, but the clear reason and the Monday offer make the no easier to accept. 🙂

subtype: Asking whether it would be a yes as a first request [Response]
passage: Bhavna, you'll laugh. My neighbour, Kusum Aunty, first asked me to water her tulsi while she was away. Easy, yes. Then to feed her cat. Fine. Then to let the plumber in. Okay. Yesterday she called: "Beta, since you're already doing so much, could you stay at my flat for the week? The house shouldn't be empty." I opened my mouth to say yes. It felt so natural, like the next stair. And then I asked myself: Minakshi, if she had asked this on day one, would you have agreed? No way. I have my own flat, my own work. So I told her, "Aunty, I'm happy to keep watering and feeding, but I can't stay over." She said, "Oh, of course." That was it. I'd built it into a huge thing in my head.

qa.q: What was the first thing Kusum Aunty asked?
qa.a: To water her tulsi while she was away.

qa.q: Why did staying at Aunty's flat feel "like the next stair" to Minakshi?
qa.a: After saying yes to the tulsi, the cat and the plumber, each new ask felt like a natural continuation, so the biggest one seemed small.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say, and why was it a good answer?
qa.a: That the watering and feeding would continue but staying over wasn't possible; it kept the fair help while refusing the step Minakshi would never have agreed to at first.

qa.q: How might Kusum Aunty have seen the requests?
qa.a: She may simply have been worried about her empty home and not noticed how much she was adding; her easy "Oh, of course" suggests she meant no pressure.

grounding: A young adult facing a step-by-step series of requests asks whether the latest would be a yes as a first request, and politely declines it.

subtype: Asking whether it would be a yes as a first request [Response]
passage: I'm Mehak, and I sit next to Sonali in the school office where we both work. On Tuesday a sales rep came in and asked her to sign the school up for a full digital-classroom package: a whole year, all classes. Sonali said no; we don't have the budget. The rep nodded sadly and said, "I understand. Then just a three-month trial for class ten?" I watched Sonali start to nod. Then she paused and said, "Give me a moment." She wrote something on a sticky note. Later I saw it: "Would I say yes if this were the first ask?" She told the rep she would bring the trial to the principal's meeting and decide with the budget in front of her. The rep left without a signature.

qa.q: What did Sonali write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Would I say yes if this were the first ask?"

qa.q: What might Sonali have been feeling when she started to nod?
qa.a: She may have felt a pull to meet the rep halfway after refusing the big package, as if the smaller trial was a fair trade.

qa.q: What choice did Sonali make instead of signing, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She took a moment, then said she would bring the trial to the principal's meeting and decide with the budget in front of her, judging the offer on its own.

qa.q: How might the sales rep see the conversation?
qa.a: The rep offered a smaller trial right after the big no and probably hoped for a quick yes, so leaving without a signature may have been disappointing.

grounding: A colleague watches a young adult pause after a big-then-small sales request and ask whether the smaller step would be a yes on its own.
